title: The Ocean That Hides a Thousand Secrets

pages.text: Outside the marine research centre in Tema, fishing canoes and cargo ships rode the bright blue swells of the Gulf of Guinea. Inside the laboratory, thirteen-year-old Tetteh and his classmate Ama stood beside a bright yellow robotic submarine called a remotely operated vehicle, or ROV.
sentences: Outside the marine research centre in Tema, fishing canoes and cargo ships rode the bright blue swells of the Gulf of Guinea.
Inside the laboratory, thirteen-year-old Tetteh and his classmate Ama stood beside a bright yellow robotic submarine called a remotely operated vehicle, or ROV.
pages.alt: Tetteh and Ama stand with Dr Akua Mensah inside a Tema marine laboratory beside a yellow robotic deep-sea ROV.

pages.text: ‘When we stand on the beach at Tema or Cape Coast,’ said Dr Akua Mensah, tapping a wall chart of the Atlantic Ocean, ‘we only see the surface. Yet the ocean averages nearly four thousand metres deep! Most of Earth’s living space hides far beneath the waves in layers that sunlight can never reach.’
sentences: ‘When we stand on the beach at Tema or Cape Coast,’ said Dr Akua Mensah, tapping a wall chart of the Atlantic Ocean, ‘we only see the surface.
Yet the ocean averages nearly four thousand metres deep!
Most of Earth’s living space hides far beneath the waves in layers that sunlight can never reach.’
pages.alt: Dr Akua Mensah points to a visual diagram of ocean depth layers from the sunlit surface down to the pitch-black abyss.

pages.text: Dr Akua dimmed the laboratory lights and started a video recorded by the yellow ROV during an Atlantic research voyage. ‘The top two hundred metres are the sunlit zone,’ she explained. ‘Here, microscopic plant-like organisms called phytoplankton use sunlight for photosynthesis, producing oxygen and feeding fish like sardines, tuna and mackerel.’
sentences: Dr Akua dimmed the laboratory lights and started a video recorded by the yellow ROV during an Atlantic research voyage.
‘The top two hundred metres are the sunlit zone,’ she explained.
‘Here, microscopic plant-like organisms called phytoplankton use sunlight for photosynthesis, producing oxygen and feeding fish like sardines, tuna and mackerel.’
pages.alt: On a large screen, silver fish swim through bright sunlit blue surface waters filled with tiny glowing green specks.

pages.text: As the ROV camera descended past two hundred metres into the twilight zone, the blue water faded to deep indigo. ‘Why don’t human divers just swim down there with scuba tanks?’ asked Tetteh. ‘Because of hydrostatic pressure,’ said Dr Akua. ‘For every ten metres you go down, the weight of the water above adds another atmosphere of pressure.’
sentences: As the ROV camera descended past two hundred metres into the twilight zone, the blue water faded to deep indigo.
‘Why don’t human divers just swim down there with scuba tanks?’ asked Tetteh.
‘Because of hydrostatic pressure,’ said Dr Akua.
‘For every ten metres you go down, the weight of the water above adds another atmosphere of pressure.’
pages.alt: The ROV camera view shows the water turning dark indigo as Tetteh asks Dr Akua a question about deep water pressure.

pages.text: ‘At one thousand metres deep,’ Dr Akua continued, ‘the ROV enters the midnight zone, where no sunlight reaches at all and the water is near freezing. There, the pressure is about one hundred times greater than the air pressure at sea level! Our ROV uses thick titanium spheres and special syntactic foam so it will not be crushed.’

pages.alt: Dr Akua points to the thick round camera housing on the yellow ROV while Ama takes notes on her tablet.

pages.text: Suddenly, in the recorded dive video, the pilots switched off the ROV’s headlamps. Ama leaned forward in surprise. Blue and green sparks flashed in the darkness like living stars! A translucent comb jelly drifted past with rainbow ripples, and a deep-sea squid released a cloud of glowing blue light.
sentences: Suddenly, in the recorded dive video, the pilots switched off the ROV’s headlamps.
Ama leaned forward in surprise.
Blue and green sparks flashed in the darkness like living stars!
A translucent comb jelly drifted past with rainbow ripples, and a deep-sea squid released a cloud of glowing blue light.
pages.alt: On the dark monitor, a deep-sea comb jelly and squid glow with vivid blue and green bioluminescent light.

pages.text: ‘That is bioluminescence,’ said Dr Akua. ‘In the twilight and midnight zones, over three-quarters of the animals make their own cold chemical light! Inside their cells, or inside helpful bacteria living in their bodies, a molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen and an enzyme called luciferase to shine without getting hot.’
sentences: ‘That is bioluminescence,’ said Dr Akua.
‘In the twilight and midnight zones, over three-quarters of the animals make their own cold chemical light!
Inside their cells, or inside helpful bacteria living in their bodies, a molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen and an enzyme called luciferase to shine without getting hot.’
pages.alt: A close view on the screen shows a deep-sea lanternfish with rows of glowing blue light organs along its belly.

pages.text: ‘Why would an animal want to glow in the dark?’ asked Ama. ‘Wouldn’t predators see it?’ ‘Different species use light in clever ways,’ Dr Akua replied. ‘The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth to attract prey. Some shrimp squirt glowing clouds to blind predators, while lanternfish glow softly on their bellies to blend in with faint light from above!’

Some shrimp squirt glowing clouds to blind predators, while lanternfish glow softly on their bellies to blend in with faint light from above!’
pages.alt: The screen displays a deep-sea anglerfish with a glowing blue lure arched above its wide jaw.

pages.text: The ROV video jumped deeper, to three thousand metres along a deep ocean ridge. Tall rocky chimneys rose from the seafloor, billowing thick dark clouds of mineral-rich water heated by magma far below the crust. ‘These are hydrothermal vents,’ said Dr Akua. ‘The water gushing out can exceed three hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, yet the crushing pressure stops it from boiling!’

Tall rocky chimneys rose from the seafloor, billowing thick dark clouds of mineral-rich water heated by magma far below the crust.
‘These are hydrothermal vents,’ said Dr Akua.
‘The water gushing out can exceed three hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, yet the crushing pressure stops it from boiling!’
pages.alt: The ROV illuminates tall rocky hydrothermal vent chimneys gushing dark mineral plumes on the ocean floor.

pages.text: In comparison footage from Pacific and Atlantic vents, Tetteh stared at the colonies of white vent crabs, pale shrimp and giant red-plumed tube worms crowded around the chimneys. ‘How can so many animals live down here with zero sunlight and no green plants?’ he asked. ‘This discovery in nineteen seventy-seven shocked biologists everywhere,’ Dr Akua said with a smile.
sentences: In comparison footage from Pacific and Atlantic vents, Tetteh stared at the colonies of white vent crabs, pale shrimp and giant red-plumed tube worms crowded around the chimneys.
‘How can so many animals live down here with zero sunlight and no green plants?’ he asked.
‘This discovery in nineteen seventy-seven shocked biologists everywhere,’ Dr Akua said with a smile.
pages.alt: Tetteh points closely at the monitor showing giant red-plumed tube worms and white crabs thriving beside a hydrothermal vent.

pages.text: ‘Instead of sunlight,’ Dr Akua explained, ‘billions of microbes around the vents use chemical energy from hydrogen sulfide dissolved in the vent water to build food. Scientists call this chemosynthesis. Those microbes form the base of an entire dark-ocean food web! It even gives astrobiologists clues about how life might survive beneath the icy oceans of moons like Europa.’

It even gives astrobiologists clues about how life might survive beneath the icy oceans of moons like Europa.’
pages.alt: Dr Akua shows a comparison chart on a tablet: surface life powered by sunlight versus deep-vent life powered by chemical energy.

pages.text: As they stepped back outside into the warm Tema sunshine, Ama looked out at the endless Atlantic horizon. ‘Dr Akua, have scientists mapped the whole ocean floor yet?’ Dr Akua shook her head. ‘More than seventy percent of the global seafloor has never been mapped in high detail, and thousands of deep-sea species await discovery. The ocean still keeps most of its secrets for your generation to explore!’ The end.

activities.question: Why does water pressure increase so rapidly as an ROV descends into the deep ocean?
options: The weight of water above adds about one atmosphere every ten metres
The ocean floor has giant magnets pulling downward
Sunlight pushes the surface water down
activities.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure comes from the weight of the water above, adding roughly one atmosphere of pressure for every 10 metres of depth.

activities.definition: The production of cold chemical light by living organisms.
distractors: Light reflected from the Moon onto ocean waves

activities.question: How does the deep-sea lanternfish use bioluminescence on its belly to survive in the twilight zone?
options: It glows softly to match faint light above and hide its shadow from below
It uses its light to perform photosynthesis
It heats up the freezing water around its fins
It signals to fishing boats on the surface
activities.explanation: Glowing on the underside (counter-illumination) breaks up the fish’s dark silhouette against faint downwelling light.

activities.question: What powers the base of the food web around deep-sea hydrothermal vents where no sunlight reaches?
options: Chemosynthetic microbes using chemical energy from hydrogen sulfide
Green seaweed growing on the hot chimneys
Dead leaves blown from coastal forests
activities.explanation: Around hydrothermal vents, chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea convert chemical energy (such as hydrogen sulfide) into organic food without sunlight.

activities.prompt: Why do you think scientists study deep-sea hydrothermal vents when preparing missions to icy moons like Jupiter’s moon Europa?
Order these ocean zones and features from shallowest to deepest as the ROV descended.
items: The sunlit zone (0 to 200 m), where phytoplankton perform photosynthesis.
The twilight zone (200 to 1,000 m), where sunlight fades to dim indigo.
The midnight zone (below 1,000 m), pitch black with crushing pressure.
Deep-sea hydrothermal vents on the ocean ridge powered by chemosynthesis.

activities.prompt: Knowing that more than seventy percent of the deep ocean floor has not yet been mapped in detail, how do you feel about future ocean exploration?

glossary.definition: Microscopic plant-like organisms drifting in sunlit surface water that make food by photosynthesis.
The continuous physical force exerted on or against an object by the weight of water or air above it.
Light produced by a chemical reaction inside a living organism.
A light-emitting compound found in organisms that produce bioluminescence.
The process by which microbes use chemical energy instead of sunlight to make food.
